questions.question: What extra condition turns a group into an Abelian group?
options: The set has exactly two elements
Every element is equal to the identity
The operation is written using addition notation

questions.question: In an Abelian group, why does the order of two factors not matter?
options: Because the identity element changes with the order
Because every operation in a group is automatically commutative

questions.question: Which group axiom is not replaced by commutativity in an Abelian group?
options: The requirement that the operation be multiplication
The requirement that all elements be positive
The need for a finite set

questions.question: Which implication is always true?
options: Every Abelian group is a group

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb R,+)$ a natural example of an Abelian group?
options: Real numbers have no additive inverses, irrespective of the particular case.
Real addition is not closed on $\mathbb R$
Real addition is associative, has identity and inverses, and is commutative
Real addition has no identity element

questions.question: In an Abelian group with operation $*$, what can replace $x*y$?
Which example is Abelian under its usual operation?
options: A group with operation $ab\ne ba$ for some $a,b$
All permutations of three objects under composition
The set of invertible $2\times2$ matrices under multiplication

questions.question: If $a+b=b+a$ for all real numbers $a,b$, which Abelian-group feature is being used in $(\mathbb R,+)$?
Suppose a group has elements $p,q$ such that $pq\ne qp$. What can be concluded?
options: The structure is not a group
The inverse of $p$ does not exist
The identity element does not exist

questions.question: In the additive group $(\mathbb R,+)$, what is the inverse of $5$?
Why is it not enough to check only $a*b=b*a$ when proving that a structure is an Abelian group?
options: A group cannot have an identity element
Commutativity is never part of Abelian groups
Only finite groups can be Abelian
One must also show the structure is a group

questions.question: Which statement best separates “group” from “Abelian group”?
options: A group must be finite; an Abelian group must be infinite
A group may be noncommutative; an Abelian group may not
A group has no inverses; an Abelian group has inverses
A group has two operations; an Abelian group has one operation

questions.question: Why is the word “Abelian” meaningful only after there is already a group operation?
options: It means the operation has no identity
It describes the size of the underlying set
It means every element is a real number
It describes commutativity of that group operation

questions.question: In an Abelian group, simplify $a*b*a^{-1}$ using commutativity.
Let $(G,*)$ be a group. Which observation proves that $G$ is not Abelian?
options: Finding an inverse for every element

questions.question: If $G$ is Abelian and $a*b=c$, what is $b*a$?
options: It cannot be determined even in an Abelian group

questions.question: Why does “every Abelian group is a group” not imply “every group is Abelian”?
options: Adding a condition gives a smaller class, not an equivalent class
Commutativity follows from associativity in every operation
The word group means exactly the same as Abelian group

questions.question: In additive notation, which identity signals the Abelian property rather than merely the existence of inverses?
Let $G$ be Abelian. If $a^2=e$, $b^3=e$, and the operation is written multiplicatively, what is $(ab)^6$?
The operation table of a group shows $r*s=t$ but $s*r=u$ with $u\ne t$. What is the best conclusion?
options: The table cannot define any group because rows differ from columns
